unit.title: Fractions as Parts of a Whole

contentBlocks.text: You've drawn and placed fractions. Today: compare two fractions to see which is bigger!

When two fractions have the same denominator (bottom number), the one with the bigger numerator (top number) is bigger — more equal-sized parts means more of the whole. 3/4 is bigger than 1/4, because 3 parts out of 4 is more than 1 part out of 4. Compare: which is bigger, 2/5 or 4/5? Draw two identical rectangles, shade 2/5 in one and 4/5 in the other, and check your answer visually.
You just compared fractions with the same denominator! Tomorrow we'll learn about fractions that look different but are actually equal.

objectives: Compare two fractions with the same denominator by comparing their numerators
Verify a fraction comparison by drawing and shading two identical shapes
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review yesterday's number-line work.
2. Introduce same-denominator comparison using the 3/4 vs. 1/4 example.
3. Have the child compare 2/5 and 4/5, drawing shaded rectangles to verify.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's equivalent-fractions lesson.
differentiationTips: Struggling: always require the visual check (drawing and shading) rather than reasoning about the numbers alone
Ready for more: ask the child to explain in their own words why a bigger numerator means a bigger fraction, when the denominator stays the same
This lesson is deliberately limited to same-denominator comparisons — comparing different denominators is a harder skill for a later grade, not this week
teacherGuide.answerKey: 4/5 is bigger than 2/5, because 4 equal parts out of 5 is more than 2 equal parts out of 5.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses Common Core Grade 3 standard 3.NF.3d: comparing two fractions with the same denominator, continuing this week's fractions thread.

generationData.instructions: Compare each pair of fractions. Write which is bigger.
